Plugins

Source: vignettes/plugins.Rmd
plugins.Rmd

EpiSODIC supports plugins: small add-ons, written by other developers or by yourself, that let EpiSODIC work with the rest of your world. Every laboratory and public health service has its own systems, its own partners and its own way of working, and no single package can know them all. A plugin closes that gap without anyone having to change EpiSODIC itself.

What a plugin can do

A plugin can put a button on an outbreak or epidemic dossier, or quietly do its work after every detection run. A few examples of what that makes possible:

  • Share an outbreak with a regional platform in one click, straight from its dossier.
  • Open a ticket in your organisation’s service desk for every outbreak that needs follow-up.
  • Notify the public health service in the format their own system expects.
  • Post a summary of each night’s run to a team chat or an internal dashboard.
  • Copy figures to a data warehouse for your own reporting.

Plugins can be written in R, Python or Bash, so whoever in your team knows any of these can make one. And because a plugin only uses what EpiSODIC has already found, it never changes what EpiSODIC detects.

EpiSODIC ships with one ready-made plugin, which sends an outbreak’s summary to a web address of your choice. It is a good first plugin to try, and a good template for a plugin of your own:

file.show(system.file("plugins", "share-outbreak-http.yaml", package = "EpiSODIC"))

Using plugins

Installing and switching on

Everything happens on the Plugins screen, which an administrator reaches from its card on the Instance screen.

  1. Install a plugin by pasting its address (a file page on GitHub will do) or the path of a file on the server. EpiSODIC checks the file before saving it, and tells you plainly if something is wrong with it.
  2. Read what it asks for. The screen lists what each plugin receives, which settings it reads and where it sends data.
  3. Enable it. EpiSODIC shows once more what you are about to allow, and the plugin is ready.

From then on, a button plugin appears on the dossiers it belongs to, for every epidemiologist. A plugin that runs after each detection run simply starts doing its work.

Disabling, updating and uninstalling are one click each on the same screen. An update that asks for more than you allowed before waits for your approval rather than quietly taking it.

What you see

Each plugin on the Plugins screen has a status:

  • Enabled: it is switched on and works.
  • Disabled: installed, but switched off.
  • Needs approval: a newer version asks for more than you allowed. Enable it again once you agree.
  • Unavailable: something is missing, such as an R package or a program it needs, and the screen says what.
  • File missing: it is switched on, but its file is gone. Nothing else is affected; the plugin simply does not run.

The same screen keeps a record of every time a plugin ran: who started it, on which outbreak, and how it went.

Pushing a plugin’s button

On a dossier, a plugin’s button does what its label says. If the plugin sends the outbreak’s case list out of EpiSODIC, it first asks you to confirm and names where the data goes. Afterwards you see the plugin’s message, often with a link to the result, such as the new ticket or the shared outbreak.

Only epidemiologists see plugin buttons; viewers and visitors who have not signed in do not.

Keeping it safe

A plugin runs its own code on your server, so treat installing one the way you would treat installing any software:

  • Install plugins only from sources you trust, and have someone read a plugin before you enable it.
  • EpiSODIC gives each plugin only what it asked for and you allowed. It never gives a plugin EpiSODIC’s own passwords or database access.
  • Every run is recorded, including what was sent and where.
  • Sending case-level data to another organisation is processing of personal data under the GDPR, plugin or not, so it needs the usual legal basis and agreement.

Working from a script

Everything the Plugins screen does is also available from R, for an administrator who prefers scripts:

episodic_plugin_install("https://github.com/org/plugins/blob/v1.0.0/share-regional.yaml")
episodic_plugin_list()
episodic_plugin_enable("share-regional")
episodic_plugin_run("share-regional", cluster_id = 12)
episodic_plugin_disable("share-regional")
episodic_plugin_uninstall("share-regional")

Plugins are kept in a folder: the one named by EPISODIC_PLUGIN_DIR, or otherwise a plugins folder beside your configuration file. Which plugins are switched on is written in that configuration file, under plugins, so it is visible and editable in the same place as all your other settings.

Developing a plugin

A plugin is one YAML file. It says what the plugin is, what it needs, and which steps it runs. Here is a complete one:

name: Share outbreak with a regional platform
version: 1.0.0
api: 1
trigger: button
placement: outbreak
label:
  en: Share with regional platform
  nl: Delen met regionaal platform
permissions: [cluster_summary]
secrets: [SHARE_ENDPOINT_URL, SHARE_ENDPOINT_TOKEN]
requires:
  packages: [httr2, jsonlite]
timeout: 60
steps:
  - name: Send the outbreak
    shell: r
    run: |
      payload <- jsonlite::read_json(Sys.getenv("EPISODIC_PAYLOAD"))
      # ... send it ...
      cat("message=Shared ", payload$cluster$label, "\n",
          sep = "", file = Sys.getenv("EPISODIC_RESULT"))

The file’s name is the plugin’s id: share-outbreak-http.yaml is the plugin share-outbreak-http. An id uses lowercase letters, digits and hyphens.

The easiest way to start is to copy the shipped plugin, give it a name of its own and change its steps. Install it from its path on the server, enable it, and push its button.

Every key

EpiSODIC checks every key. A key it does not know is reported rather than ignored, so a typo shows up on the Plugins screen straight away.

Key Required What it holds
name yes The plugin’s name, as the Plugins screen shows it
version yes The plugin’s own version
api yes The plugin API version it was written for; this EpiSODIC provides 1
trigger yes button, or run_committed to run after every detection run
steps yes The steps it runs, in order
placement for a button outbreak or epidemic: the dossier the button is on
label for a button The button’s text per language; en is required and used when a language is missing
description no A description per language, with en
permissions no The parts of the data it receives (see below)
destination with cluster_cases Where it sends data, in words, shown before every send
secrets no Names of the server’s environment variables it may read
requires no packages (R packages) and commands (programs on the PATH) it needs
timeout no Seconds the whole plugin may run, 1 to 600; 60 by default
source no An https:// address of the plugin itself, from which the Plugins screen updates it

Requirements are checked, never installed: a plugin whose package or program is missing is listed as unavailable, with the reason, until the server has what it needs.

Steps

Each step has a shell (r, bash or python) and the code it runs, and may have a name and plain settings in env:

steps:
  - name: Prepare
    shell: r
    run: |
      writeLines("prepared", "state.txt")
  - name: Upload
    shell: bash
    env:
      MODE: production
    run: |
      curl --fail --silent -T state.txt "$UPLOAD_TARGET"
      echo "message=Uploaded" >> "$EPISODIC_RESULT"

r runs with the same R installation and packages as EpiSODIC; bash and python use the programs on the server. Steps share one working folder, so one step can leave a file for the next. A step that fails ends the plugin there, and its error is recorded.

Placeholders

A step’s env can take values from the payload with placeholders, which saves reading the payload file for a value or two:

    env:
      TITLE: "Outbreak ${{ cluster.label }}: ${{ cluster.pathogen }}"
      SENT_BY: ${{ user.username }}

A placeholder names a path in the payload (below), and only parts the plugin receives: cluster needs cluster_summary, run needs run_summary, and cases, being a list, cannot be used. A placeholder whose value is missing in a run stops that run and says which one, rather than passing an empty value.

Placeholders work in env only, never in run. The filled value reaches your code as an environment variable, as data, so a ward or pathogen name can never change what the code does. A ${{ }} in run is reported as a mistake.

What a step receives

Each step runs in a fresh process with:

  • EPISODIC_PAYLOAD: the path of a JSON file with the data the plugin may see (below).
  • EPISODIC_RESULT: the path of the file it reports back to (below).
  • EPISODIC_PLUGIN_ID and EPISODIC_LANGUAGE: the plugin’s id, and the language of whoever pushed the button, so a message can be written in that language.
  • The plugin’s secrets, once enabled, and the step’s own env.
  • What a program needs to start and to reach the network: PATH, HOME, the locale, proxy settings and certificate stores.

Nothing else from the server’s environment is passed, and none of EpiSODIC’s own variables ever is: a secret whose name starts with EPISODIC_ is refused.

The payload

The payload always holds api, plugin (id, version), trigger, instance_id, language and dashboard_url, and for a button the user who pushed it (username, role). The rest depends on the plugin’s permissions; a part it has no permission for is simply absent:

Permission Trigger Adds
cluster_summary button cluster: its id and label (O-12, in the reader’s language), scale, origin, pathogen, level, care line, region, institution, ward, first and last day, counts, expected, excess, ratio, priority score, detector agreement, opening time and the latest classification
cluster_cases button cases: the cluster’s cases as stored, pseudonymised, one object per case
run_summary run_committed run: its id, date, status, whether it was the first run on the database, its counts, and new_clusters with the summary of each cluster it opened

cluster_cases is the one permission that sends case-level data. A plugin that asks for it must say where the data goes in destination, and EpiSODIC asks for confirmation, naming that destination, every time its button is pushed.

Reporting back

A step reports by adding lines to the file in EPISODIC_RESULT:

status=success
message=O-12 was shared.
link=https://regional.example/outbreaks/123

status is success (the default) or error, when the plugin wants to say that what it tried did not work. message is one line of text, and link an http or https address the dashboard offers as a link. A later line overrides an earlier one, and any other line is reported as a mistake in the plugin. A plugin that reports nothing and finishes cleanly has succeeded without a message.

The dashboard shows the message as plain text and the link as a plain link, never as markup.

When something goes wrong

A plugin that fails, or runs longer than its timeout, is stopped and recorded, with the end of its error output. Whoever pushed the button sees that output straight away, and an administrator finds it on the Plugins screen, always with the values of the plugin’s secrets masked. A plugin that runs after detection runs can never make a run fail, and one failing plugin never stops the others.

Limitations

What a plugin cannot do, by design:

  • It never receives EpiSODIC’s own settings or credentials (the database, mail, Microsoft 365 or the import and export keys), so it cannot read or write the database, send mail through EpiSODIC’s channels, or create an export file of its own.
  • It works with what its permissions put in the payload: a cluster’s summary and cases, or a run’s summary. Anything else EpiSODIC holds is out of its reach.
  • It cannot change what EpiSODIC detects, how clusters are reconciled or how they are assessed: it acts on results, never on detection.
  • It cannot add screens or panels to the dashboard; a button plugin adds a button and shows a message and a link.
  • It cannot install software: what it requires must already be on the server.
  • It runs for at most 600 seconds, and a button plugin keeps the person who pushed it waiting until it finishes.
  • Every secret it names must be set on the server; there are no optional secrets.
  • It cannot be trusted further than its own code: EpiSODIC narrows what a plugin receives and records what it did, but cannot stop it sending what it received somewhere other than its destination says.

Versions

The plugin API version changes only when the file format, the payload or the result changes incompatibly. A plugin written for another version is listed as unavailable with the reason, rather than handed data it might misread. When you publish a plugin, point its source at a release tag or commit rather than a branch, so an update is a deliberate step for everyone who uses it.
